boundary_rationale: This row is the book's title line and stands alone as its own parent: “The Song of songs, which is Solomon’s.” (web:Song.1.1) renders שִׁ֥יר הַשִּׁירִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר לִשְׁלֹמֹֽה (oshb:Song.1.1, tier: byte). The verse opens with the construct superlative שִׁ֥יר הַשִּׁירִ֖ים and carries the relative-pronoun clause אֲשֶׁ֥ר לִשְׁלֹמֹֽה (oshb:Song.1.1, tier: byte, 'which is Solomon's', a form occurring exactly once book-wide: sweep 1 verse); no verse before it and no verse after it shares this header form, so the seam at Song.1.1|Song.1.2 rests on the frame architecture rather than on any voice marker.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Song.1.1 as a non-counted title pseudo-verse fused into the opening lyric address was rejected: both witnesses count it as an ordinary verse, and it is the verse the two-parent frame (F1/M) sets apart as the header, distinct from the surrounding lyric corpus.

device_notes: Texture: elsewhere the book's relative particle is the she-prefix; the superscription attributes the collection to Solomon. No parashah mark touches this verse in the WLC inventory.

boundary_rationale: This unit opens the lyric corpus with the woman's voice addressing the man throughout: טוֹבִ֥ים דֹּדֶ֖יךָ (oshb:Song.1.2, tier: byte, 'your loves [are] better') carries a second-masculine-singular possessive suffix, and the unit's second verse opens מָשְׁכֵ֖נִי אַחֲרֶ֣יךָ (oshb:Song.1.4, tier: byte, 'draw me after you'), a matching second-masculine-singular imperative-plus-suffix address. The addressee stays constant (2ms 'you') across all three verses even where the grammatical person of the speaker shifts to the cohortative 'we' of “We will be glad and rejoice in you.” (web:Song.1.4); that person-shift is disclosed as texture below rather than argued as a voice-shift, since no addressee or gender-marked form changes.
